[p. 3] [...] There is also a pattern in the stress which occurs on verbs, though this is not actually marked on the chart: 5a. For distant past tense and both present tenses stress always falls on the tense marker. 5b. For near past tense and all imperatives stress always falls on the final syllable of the stem. The one exception to this is that for second singular emphatic imperative the stress falls on the first syllable of the stem. 5c. For future tense, customary aspect and subjunctive mood stress always falls on the final syllable. [p. 16]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Umbu-Ungu (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Head supplies the first primary statement: stress is phonemic/contrastive, morphologically governed on verbs (tense-marker vs stem-final vs word-final by tense/mood), word-final on pronouns, unpredictable in other roots. Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic (contrastive) and is written only to separate otherwise identical forms; in non-verb roots its position is not predictable from syllable count (the compound table on p. 9 gives ámbo, kángo, kúmbi, wále, óla with initial stress beside kolá, ulké, keré with final stress, and compounds yémbo, ambolángo, koláulke, kumbikeré, walsé, wélela with stress on initial, penult, second, or final syllable, with 'change of stress' signalling compounding). In verbs stress is morphologically fixed: on the tense marker in distant past and both present tenses (kano-rú-mbulu, kano-kó-ro, kano-pá-ro), on the final syllable of the stem in near past and imperatives (kanó-mbulu, sí-mbulu), and on the final syllable of the word in future, customary and subjunctive (kano-ngé, kano-mbá). Pronouns: 'Stress always falls on the final syllable of every form' (p. 23). Two-part words like suku singi are counted as separate words 'because both suku and singi take word stress' (p. 27).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 35: the verbal negative naa 'functions like a prefix to the verb; that is, it takes a stress so strong that the stress of the verb following becomes either secondary or is lost all together so that the negator plus the verb functions as one phonological word'; p. 57 rule 3: 'Heavy phrase stress falls on the verbal negative.' Connectors 'take very low intonation and virtually no stress' (p. 33), pause words omba, ndemele 'are stressless' (p. 35), Connective Complexes 'are virtually stressless' (p. 56); molo 'or' has 'virtually no stress' while molo 'no' 'has strong word-initial stress' (p. 195 fn 20).
new_statements.exceptions: Second singular emphatic imperative stresses the first syllable of the stem (p. 16). Compounding shifts stress (p. 9). Back vowels in word-final unstressed syllables after nasals are usually dropped (p. 169). Stress written in the orthography only for minimal pairs (p. 3).
new_statements.identity_note: Head (p. 1) describes 'the Umbu-Ungu dialect of the Kaugel language' (Kaugel = Gawigl of Wurm 1982), and 'specifically reflects the Kala sub-dialect of the Umbu-Ungu dialect of Kaugel which is spoken in and near Palinoli village' (Tambul District, Western Highlands); the future-tense allomorphy note refers to 'the sub-dialect under study' (p. 18). Throughout the text she calls the language 'Kaugel', so quotes naming Kaugel are about Umbu-Ungu (umbu1258). Blowers 1970 is titled 'Kaugel verb morphology' and may describe a neighbouring Kaugel/Gawigl variety rather than Umbu-Ungu proper; it is offered only as corroboration.
